headline: Jackery's Newest Power Bank Is Small, Powerful, and Built to Last for Years

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called Jackery makes small boxes that store electricity, called power stations. You can use them to charge your phone, tablet, or other devices when you are not near a plug, like on an airplane or during a camping trip. Jackery just made its smallest power station ever. It is called the Explorer 100D. It is about the size of a small water bottle and weighs less than two pounds, so it is easy to carry in a backpack or suitcase. Even though it is tiny, it can charge phones and other gadgets many times before running out of power. Inside, it uses a special kind of battery called LFP, which stands for lithium iron phosphate. This battery type is safer and can be used over and over again for about eight years before it wears out. The power station costs $99 at Walmart, or you can buy two together at Costco. You can even charge it using sunlight with a solar panel if you do not have a plug nearby. This makes it great for travel, emergencies, or outdoor adventures.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Jackery, a company that makes portable chargers, just released its smallest power station yet, called the Explorer 100D. It measures only about 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighs under two pounds, making it small enough to fit in a carry-on bag for a flight or a backpack for a hike. Despite its tiny size, it holds 96 watt-hours of energy, which is enough to charge a phone many times over. What makes this power station special is the type of battery inside it. It uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, which are safer than regular lithium-ion batteries found in many devices and last much longer. Jackery says the battery should work well for up to eight years and can be recharged about 3,000 times before wearing out. That is far more than cheaper portable chargers typically offer. The Explorer 100D has three charging ports: two USB-C ports and one USB-A port, though if you use all three at once, the charging speed slows down to share power evenly. It can also be charged using a solar panel, reaching 80 percent power in about 90 minutes if you have access to sunlight. The device comes with a handle, and you can buy an extra strap to carry it like a bag. It will be sold at Walmart for $99 starting November 15th, or in a two-pack at Costco for about $180. This makes high-quality, long-lasting battery technology more affordable and portable for everyday use.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Jackery, a company known for making portable power stations, has introduced its smallest and lightest model yet: the Explorer 100D. It measures just 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighs under two pounds, making it easy to pack for flights, road trips, or emergencies. Despite its compact size, it stores 96 watt-hours of energy, enough to charge smartphones, tablets, or small gadgets multiple times. What sets the Explorer 100D apart from typical portable chargers is its use of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells, a safer and more durable alternative to the lithium-ion batteries found in most consumer electronics. Lithium-ion batteries can degrade faster and, in rare cases, pose fire risks if damaged. LFP batteries are considered more stable and are rated for about 3,000 charge cycles, meaning they could last roughly eight years with regular use, according to Jackery. This longevity is a major selling point, since most basic portable chargers wear out much sooner. The device includes two USB-C ports capable of up to 140 watts each and one 18-watt USB-A port, but the total output caps at 158 watts. This means that if all three ports are used simultaneously, the charging speed for each device decreases, since the power station has to split its energy. For eco-conscious users, the Explorer 100D also supports solar charging, accepting up to 100 watts of solar input and reaching 80 percent charge in about 90 minutes with a compatible solar panel, which Jackery sells separately. Jackery emphasizes portability by including a built-in handle and offering an optional shoulder strap. The Explorer 100D will launch on November 15th for $99 through Walmart, while Costco already offers it in a two-pack for $179.99. This pricing makes the LFP battery technology—typically found in larger, more expensive power stations—accessible in a smaller, budget-friendly format. As more people rely on personal electronics while traveling or during power outages, compact and dependable charging solutions like this reflect a growing demand for portable energy that is both efficient and long-lasting.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Jackery, a company specializing in portable power stations, has unveiled its smallest device to date: the Explorer 100D. Measuring just 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing under two pounds, it is compact enough to fit in a carry-on bag, yet it stores 96 watt-hours of energy—enough to recharge phones, tablets, and other small devices multiple times during travel or outdoor activities. What distinguishes this model from typical portable chargers is its battery chemistry. The Explorer 100D uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, a technology Jackery first adopted in 2023. Unlike the more common lithium-ion batteries found in most consumer electronics, LFP batteries are considered safer, more thermally stable, and significantly more durable. Jackery states that these cells are engineered to last roughly eight years with regular use and can endure about 3,000 charge cycles before their capacity noticeably declines. This is a meaningful upgrade over cheaper portable chargers, which often lose efficiency after a few hundred charges. In terms of charging capability, the device includes two 140-watt USB-C ports and one 18-watt USB-A port, but its total output is capped at 158 watts. This means that when multiple devices are charging simultaneously, the available power is distributed among them, reducing the speed at which each device charges. The Explorer 100D also supports solar charging, accepting up to 100 watts of solar input and reaching 80 percent capacity in about 90 minutes under good sunlight conditions, provided users also carry a compatible solar panel. This feature appeals to campers, hikers, or those preparing for power outages who want a backup energy source that does not rely solely on electrical outlets. Despite its reduced size, Jackery maintained practical design features such as an integrated handle, along with an optional shoulder strap for easier transport. The Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15th through Walmart for $99, while Costco already sells it in a two-pack for $179.99 for customers who do not want to wait. This release reflects a broader trend in consumer electronics: manufacturers are increasingly prioritizing battery longevity and safety, not just affordability or capacity, as portable power becomes essential for remote work, travel, and emergency preparedness. By offering LFP technology at a relatively low price point, Jackery is making more durable and safer battery systems accessible to a wider range of everyday users, potentially reducing electronic waste from frequently replaced lower-quality chargers.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Jackery, a company that has built its reputation around portable power stations for travel, outdoor recreation, and emergency preparedness, has released its smallest and lightest model yet: the Explorer 100D. Measuring a mere 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing under two pounds, the device is compact enough to meet airline carry-on restrictions while still delivering 96 watt-hours (30,000mAh) of stored energy—sufficient to recharge smartphones and small electronics multiple times over the course of a long flight or outdoor trip. What makes this release notable is not merely its size, but the battery chemistry powering it. The Explorer 100D uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells, technology Jackery first introduced in 2023 and has since expanded across its product line. LFP batteries differ from the lithium-ion cells found in most consumer electronics by offering greater thermal stability, reduced fire risk, and a substantially longer usable lifespan. According to Jackery, the cells in the Explorer 100D are engineered for roughly eight years of regular use and can withstand approximately 3,000 charge cycles before their performance meaningfully declines. This is a considerable improvement over conventional lithium-ion power banks, which often degrade after a few hundred cycles, contributing to a cycle of frequent replacement and electronic waste. In terms of charging infrastructure, the device offers two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts each and a single 18-watt USB-A port, though the unit's total output is capped at 158 watts. Consequently, when all three ports are used simultaneously, the available power must be divided among connected devices, resulting in slower charging speeds for each. This design trade-off reflects the broader engineering challenge of maximizing both portability and output in increasingly compact devices. The Explorer 100D also supports solar charging, accepting up to 100 watts of direct solar input and reaching 80 percent capacity in approximately 90 minutes under optimal sunlight—an appealing feature for users who want energy independence from traditional power grids, whether for environmental reasons or practical necessity during power outages or remote travel. Despite its reduced footprint, Jackery retained user-friendly design elements, including a built-in carrying handle and an optional shoulder strap, underscoring the company's continued emphasis on portability even as it shrinks the device's overall size. Pricing reflects an effort to balance advanced battery technology with accessibility: the Explorer 100D will be available beginning November 15th through Walmart for $99, while Costco already offers it in a two-pack for $179.99 for buyers who do not wish to wait. This launch is emblematic of a broader shift within the consumer electronics industry, where manufacturers are increasingly competing not just on price or capacity, but on durability, safety, and environmental sustainability. As reliance on personal electronic devices grows across both everyday life and emergency scenarios, the demand for compact, long-lasting, and safer power solutions is likely to continue shaping product development across the industry.

questions: If you could only bring one small gadget on a trip to keep your devices charged, would battery life and safety matter more to you than price? Why?
How might longer-lasting batteries, like the ones in this new power station, affect how much electronic waste people create over time?
In what situations at school, at home, or during travel do you think having a reliable backup power source could be especially helpful?
